present.explain: A Russian verb's ending says who does it: я пью (I drink), ты пьёшь (you drink), он пьёт (he drinks); я чита́ю, ты чита́ешь, она́ чита́ет; я иду́, ты идёшь, мы идём, вы идёте. Learn each verb's forms as you meet them: пить and идти́ change more than their ending.
present.why: English changes its verb only for he and she; Russian changes it for everyone, so [[пью]] already says I drink. The same form says I drink and I'm drinking: Russian has no -ing.

examples.text: Мы идём домой, а он читает.
examples.means: We're going home, and he's reading.
examples.literal: We go home, and he reads.

contrasts.says: English adds -s only for he and she, and says I'm drinking with -ing; Russian has one form for both, with an ending for each person.
After хочу́ or могу́, the next verb takes no ending: Я хочу́ пить.

mistakes.why: With я, it's пью.
With ты, it's чита́ешь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

gender.explain: Every Russian noun is a он word, a она́ word or an оно́ word, and the words with it match: оди́н чай, одна́ маши́на; мой телефо́н, моя́ маши́на. Most nouns ending in a consonant are он words (телефо́н, ключ, дом), most ending in -а are она́ words (су́мка, маши́на, ма́ма), and most ending in -о are оно́ words (молоко́). ко́фе is a он word though it ends in -е.
gender.why: English has he, she and it for people and for what you point back to; Russian sorts every noun this way, so a phone is он: Где телефо́н? [[Он]] здесь. Learn which with the word; the ending usually tells you.

examples.means: My coffee is on the table.

contrasts.says: English calls a thing it; Russian calls a телефо́н он and a су́мка она́, as it would a man and a woman.
мой and твой follow the noun's gender: мой ключ, моя́ су́мка.

mistakes.why: телефо́н is a он word: мой.
чай is a он word: оди́н.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

no-be.explain: In the present, Russian says no am, is or are: Я до́ма (I'm at home), Телефо́н на столе́ (the phone is on the table), Где ключ? (where's the key?). The words just stand side by side.
no-be.why: English needs a verb in every sentence; Russian leaves to be out in the present, as an English headline does (Phone on table).

contrasts.says: English can't leave is out (The phone on the table isn't a sentence); Russian always does in the present.
Э́то alone says this is: Э́то мой ключ (this my key).

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

question.explain: A yes/no question keeps a statement's order; only the voice rises on the word asked about (the ? when written): Маши́на здесь. (the car's here) → Маши́на здесь? (is the car here?). A question word (где, что, чей) most often comes first: Где маши́на? Что ты чита́ешь?
question.why: English turns words around or adds do (Do you drink coffee?); Russian changes nothing but the voice: Ты пьёшь ко́фе? There's no do in Russian at all.

contrasts.says: English moves is or adds do (Is the car here? Do you read?); Russian keeps the order and lets the voice ask.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

accusative.explain: What you drink, read or hold takes the accusative. For она́ words ending in -а, the -а becomes -у: вода́ → Я пью во́ду, кни́га → Я чита́ю кни́гу, газе́та → Он чита́ет газе́ту. он and оно́ words stay as they are: Я пью чай, Я пью молоко́.
accusative.why: English shows who does what by order alone; Russian also marks it on the word, so [[во́ду]] is water as what's drunk, wherever it stands.

contrasts.says: English never changes water for what you drink; Russian does: вода́, во́ду.
Where something is takes -е instead: в маши́не, на столе́.

mistakes.why: What you drink: во́ду.
What he reads: кни́гу.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

prepositional.explain: After в (in) and на (on, at), where something is takes the prepositional, mostly ending in -е: стол → на столе́, су́мка → в су́мке, маши́на → в маши́не, рабо́та → на рабо́те.
prepositional.why: English says where with in and on alone; Russian says it twice, with the little word and with the ending, so [[столе́]] after на is the table as a place.

examples.means: The key is on the table.
The phone is in the bag.

contrasts.says: English's on and in change nothing after them; Russian's change the word.
до́ма (at home) and домо́й (home, going there) say it without в or на.

mistakes.why: After в, where it is: су́мке.
After на, where she is: рабо́те.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

possessive.explain: мой (my) and твой (your) match their noun as an adjective does: мой телефо́н, моя́ су́мка; твой ключ, твоя́ маши́на. твой is for someone you say ты to.
possessive.why: English's my never changes; Russian's follows the noun's gender, so [[моя́]] tells you су́мка is a она́ word.

examples.means: Your bag is on the table.

contrasts.says: The noun's gender decides: мой for он words, моя́ for она́ words.
English has one my; Russian has мой and моя́, and more forms you'll meet.

mistakes.why: ключ is a он word: мой.
су́мка is a она́ word: твоя́.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

short-adjective.explain: A few adjectives have a short form for how someone is, and it says the gender: гото́в (a man), гото́ва (a woman), гото́вы (more than one, or вы). Я гото́в. Она́ гото́ва. Мы гото́вы.
short-adjective.why: English's ready is the same for everyone; Russian's says who it's about, so a woman says Я [[гото́ва]] and a man Я гото́в.

contrasts.says: English says ready for anyone; Russian's form says a man, a woman or more than one.
With вы, even to one person, it's гото́вы.

mistakes.why: With мы: гото́вы.
With она́: гото́ва.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

direction.explain: Being somewhere and going there are different words: до́ма is at home, домо́й is home as where you go: Я до́ма (I'm at home), Я иду́ домо́й (I'm going home).
direction.why: English uses home for both; Russian asks where at or where to. A verb of going takes [[домо́й]]; being, drinking or reading there takes до́ма.

contrasts.says: English's home is both; Russian's до́ма is where you are and домо́й where you go.
идти́ (to go) takes домо́й: Я иду́ домо́й.

mistakes.why: Where you are: до́ма.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

ne.explain: не goes right before the word it denies, most often the verb: Я не пью ко́фе (I don't drink coffee), Я не могу́ помо́чь (I can't help). Russian has no do: не alone says don't.
ne.why: English needs do to say not (I don't drink); Russian puts [[не]] in front of the verb and changes nothing else.

contrasts.says: English adds do or does (I don't, she doesn't); Russian never does.
With nothing to have, нет takes есть's place: У меня́ нет рабо́ты.

mistakes.why: Before a verb it's не; нет is no.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

infinitive.explain: After хочу́ (I want), могу́ (I can) and дава́й (let's), the next verb stays in its dictionary form: Я хочу́ пить, Я могу́ помо́чь, Дава́й пить чай.
infinitive.why: English says to after want (I want to drink) and nothing after can; Russian needs neither: the dictionary form, like [[пить]], does it.

contrasts.says: Only the first verb takes the ending: Я хочу́ пить.
English adds to after want; Russian adds nothing.

mistakes.why: After хочу́, the dictionary form: пить.
After могу́: помо́чь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

have.explain: To say you have something, Russian says it's at you: У меня́ есть рабо́та (at me is work: I have work), У тебя́ есть маши́на? (do you have a car?). With none, нет takes есть's place, and the thing takes the genitive: У меня́ нет рабо́ты.
have.why: English's have is a verb of its own; Russian builds it from у (at) and меня́ (me), so У меня́ есть is I have, and the thing you have is the sentence's subject.

examples.means: I still have work to do.

contrasts.says: English's have is a verb; Russian says the thing is at you.
With нет, the thing takes the genitive: рабо́та becomes рабо́ты.

mistakes.why: What you have stays as it is: рабо́та.
After у, я becomes меня́.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: э́тот (this) matches its noun: э́тот телефо́н, э́та су́мка. э́то on its own says this is or that's, with no is, and never changes: Э́то мой ключ, Э́то су́мка ма́мы.
demonstrative.why: English says this for both; Russian's э́тот points at a thing and matches it, and э́то presents one: Э́то [[маши́на]] ма́мы (this is Mom's car).

contrasts.says: After its noun, мой or моя́ alone says mine: Э́тот телефо́н мой.
Э́то alone says this is.

mistakes.why: су́мка is a она́ word: э́та.
телефо́н is a он word: э́тот.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

address.explain: ты is for one person you know well; вы is for someone you don't know well, or for more than one, and takes the plural verb form: Ты идёшь домо́й? to a friend, Вы идёте домо́й? to a stranger or to two friends.
address.why: English has one you; Russian chooses, and the verb's ending follows: вы [[идёте]].

contrasts.says: English's you is one word for everyone; Russian's says how well you know them, or that there's more than one.
With вы, even to one person, it's гото́вы.

mistakes.why: With вы: идёте.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons, open to correction.

question-word.explain: Кто asks who, что what, где where, куда́ where to, отку́да where from, когда́ when and почему́ why. Usually start with the question word. Either the subject or the verb can follow: Куда́ ты идёшь? Куда́ идёт твой друг? Both orders are normal. If кто itself is the subject, the verb is singular: Кто стучи́т? A question about a place needs no is: Где ключ?
question-word.why: English often adds do or moves an auxiliary before the subject. Russian adds no do: Что ты и́щешь? The question word says what information is missing. Where has three useful counterparts: где for a location, куда́ for a destination, отку́да for a starting point.

contrasts.says: English often changes the order and adds do. Russian uses its ordinary verb form: Что ты чита́ешь?
Где asks about a location, as in Где твой дом? Куда́ asks about a destination, as in Куда́ ты идёшь? Отку́да asks about a starting point.
Ты стучи́шь? asks for yes or no. Кто стучи́т? asks for the person. Question words can also come later for emphasis or a follow-up: Ты куда́?

mistakes.why: When кто is the subject, use the third-person singular стучи́т, even when asking the listener who is knocking.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

pronoun-object.explain: When a pronoun names the person heard or seen, it takes its accusative form: я → меня́, ты → тебя́, он → его́, она́ → её, мы → нас, вы → вас, они́ → их. Ты меня́ слы́шишь? means Can you hear me? Я тебя́ ви́жу means I can see you. These forms often come before the verb; they can come after it too. The verb still agrees with the subject: я слы́шу, ты слы́шишь, она́ слы́шит.
pronoun-object.why: English changes I to me and he to him. Russian changes you too: ты becomes тебя́ when someone hears or sees you. The ending tells you the role even when the order changes: Ты меня́ слы́шишь? and Ты слы́шишь меня́? can both ask Can you hear me?

contrasts.says: English normally puts me after hear. Russian often puts меня́ before слы́шишь. Neither position is compulsory in Russian.
For the person heard or seen, use тебя́: Я тебя́ ви́жу. For the person receiving help, use тебе́: Я могу́ тебе́ помо́чь. Learn the form with the verb.
Use тебя́ with a friend you call ты. Use вас for someone you call вы, whether one person politely or several people.

mistakes.why: The person heard is the direct object: меня́, not the dative мне.
The person seen takes тебя́, not the dative тебе́.
Она́ is a subject form; the woman heard takes её.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

ni-ne.explain: Ничего́ and никогда́ work with the negative verb. Say Я ничего́ не хочу́ and Я никогда́ не пью ко́фе. The не stays even though English often uses a single word such as nothing or never. Nothing as an object here is ничего́. Не́чего belongs to a different construction; it cannot replace ничего́ in these sentences. A short reply can be just Ничего́: there is no verb to negate.
ni-ne.why: English can say I want nothing or I do not want anything. Russian uses ничего́ with не in the same clause. This does not turn the meaning positive. With never, keep both parts too: никогда́ не.

contrasts.says: Never already makes an English sentence negative. Russian still puts не before the verb: Я никогда́ не пью ко́фе.
Нет says there is none: У меня́ нет де́нег. A verb such as хочу́ instead uses не: Я ничего́ не хочу́.

mistakes.why: Никогда́ goes with не before the verb in this negative statement.
The object meaning not anything is ничего́ here, not не́чего.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

chto-clause.explain: Start with what someone thinks, knows or says, then use что to introduce the statement: Я ду́маю, что ма́ма уже́ до́ма. The statement can have its own subject: Я зна́ю, что ты рабо́таешь. Its verb agrees with that subject, not with the speaker of the first clause. Present-tense am, is and are are still left out: Я зна́ю, что ма́ма до́ма. A comma goes before что. In conversation, что can sometimes be omitted; these examples practice the version with it.
chto-clause.why: English often leaves out that: I think Mom is at home. Russian can make the link explicit with что. Time can set the scene before place, as in Я ду́маю, что встре́ча сего́дня в о́фисе, but Russian has no fixed rule that time must come first.

examples.text: Я думаю, что мама уже дома.
examples.means: I think Mom is already at home.
examples.literal: I think, that Mom already at home.

examples.text: Он говорит, что мама живёт в городе.
examples.means: He says Mom lives in the city.
examples.literal: He says, that Mom lives in city.

examples.text: Я думаю, что встреча сегодня в офисе.
examples.means: I think the meeting is in the office today.
examples.literal: I think, that meeting today in office.

examples.text: Я знаю, что ты сейчас гуляешь в парке.
examples.means: I know you're walking in the park now.
examples.literal: I know, that you now walk in park.

contrasts.says: Что ты чита́ешь? asks what you are reading. In Я ду́маю, что ма́ма уже́ до́ма, что introduces the statement being thought about.
Time and place can set the scene: Я ду́маю, что встре́ча сего́дня в о́фисе. Another order may put a different detail in focus; changing the order alone does not make a mistake.

mistakes.wrong: Я зна́ю, что ты сейча́с гуля́ю в па́рке.
mistakes.right: Я зна́ю, что ты сейча́с гуля́ешь в па́рке.
mistakes.why: The second subject is ты, so its verb is гуля́ешь. Я in the first clause does not control that verb.

mistakes.wrong: Он говори́т, что ма́ма живу́ в го́роде.
mistakes.right: Он говори́т, что ма́ма живёт в го́роде.
mistakes.why: Ма́ма is the subject inside the second clause, so use живёт.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

because.explain: Почему́ asks for a reason. Introduce the answer with потому́ что: Я опа́здываю, потому́ что не могу́ найти́ ключ. The phrase links a statement to its reason; it does not change the verb endings. Each clause can have its own subject. If the subject is unchanged and clear, it can be left out of the reason, as in this example. In this ordinary use, the comma comes before потому́ что, not between its two words.
because.why: English because corresponds to the two-word phrase потому́ что. Learn it together. The reason can describe an action, a location or a state: Я не могу́ помо́чь, потому́ что я за́нят. A woman says занята́.

examples.text: Я опаздываю, потому что не могу найти ключ.
examples.means: I'm running late because I can't find the key.
examples.literal: I run late, because not can find key.

examples.text: Мой друг опаздывает, потому что он у врача.
examples.means: My friend is running late because he's at the doctor's.
examples.literal: My friend runs late, because he at doctor's.

examples.text: Мама опаздывает, потому что не может найти телефон.
examples.means: Mom is running late because she can't find her phone.
examples.literal: Mom runs late, because not can find phone.

examples.text: Я хочу остаться дома, потому что здесь тихо.
examples.means: I want to stay at home because it is quiet here.
examples.literal: I want stay at home, because here quiet.

contrasts.says: Почему́ ты опа́здываешь? is the question. Я опа́здываю, потому́ что не могу́ найти́ ключ gives the reason.
Я ду́маю, что ма́ма уже́ до́ма reports a thought. Я опа́здываю, потому́ что не могу́ найти́ ключ gives a cause. Что alone and потому́ что do different jobs.

mistakes.wrong: Ты опа́здываешь, потому́ что ты рабо́таю в о́фисе?
mistakes.right: Ты опа́здываешь, потому́ что ты рабо́таешь в о́фисе?
mistakes.why: The reason has subject ты, so its verb is рабо́таешь. Потому́ что does not change the agreement.

mistakes.wrong: Я не могу́ помо́чь, потому́ что я за́няты.
mistakes.right: Я не могу́ помо́чь, потому́ что я за́нят.
mistakes.why: The reason still describes one speaker: за́нят for a man, занята́ for a woman, not the plural за́няты.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

verb-case.explain: Learn a verb together with the form of its object. For a person you are waiting for, ждать uses the accusative: Я жду тебя́, Мы ждём вас. For a person receiving help, помога́ть and помо́чь use the dative: Я помога́ю тебе́, Я могу́ помо́чь ма́ме. Neither needs a preposition for that person. This rule for ждать concerns people; it is not a claim that everything waited for always has the same case.
verb-case.why: English wait for needs for, while Russian ждёт can take the person directly. English help you has no to, while Russian still uses the dative тебе́. Translate the whole construction, not each English preposition separately.

contrasts.says: Тебя́ is the person heard or seen, and also the person waited for: Я тебя́ ви́жу; Я жду тебя́.
Тебе́ marks the person receiving help: Я помога́ю тебе́. The same case follows помо́чь: Я могу́ тебе́ помо́чь.

mistakes.why: The person waited for takes the object form тебя́, not the subject form ты.
Помога́ть takes the dative for the person helped: тебе́.
Помо́чь also takes the dative: ма́ме.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

genitive-plural.explain: A plural noun has different forms for different jobs. Год means year; after пять or ско́лько, use the genitive plural лет. Compare Ему́ три го́да with Ему́ пять лет. Age puts the person in the dative: ему́, сы́ну. A familiar example of the same case is У меня́ нет де́нег: де́ньги changes to де́нег after нет. Learn the genitive plural with each noun; the form cannot always be guessed from the ordinary plural. Quantities such as many and how many also use this case with countable things. The next lesson practices that pattern with books.
genitive-plural.why: English keeps years in both three years and five years. Russian distinguishes три го́да and пять лет. The case links the noun to the quantity. In an age expression, English makes the person the subject and adds is and old; Russian instead uses the dative person and the number of years.

examples.literal: How many years to your son?

examples.means: My son is already five years old.
examples.literal: To my son already five years.

contrasts.says: Де́ньги is the ordinary plural form. After нет, use the genitive plural де́нег.
Три го́да uses the genitive singular, but пять лет uses the genitive plural. Learn both forms with год.

mistakes.why: After пять, years has the genitive plural лет, not the singular form го́да.
Нет selects the genitive. The genitive plural of де́ньги is де́нег.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

numbers.explain: For these basic counts, one uses a singular noun and agrees with its gender: оди́н стол, одна́ кни́га. Two, three and four take the genitive singular; here practice два стола́, три стола́ and две кни́ги. Five takes the genitive plural: пять столо́в, пять книг. The form кни́ги here is genitive singular even though the same written form can also mean books elsewhere. Два is used with masculine and neuter nouns, две with feminine nouns. If the noun is understood, leave it out: У тебя́ одна́ кни́га, а у меня́ две. Larger numbers and counts after prepositions need further patterns; this lesson is about the basic counts shown here.
numbers.why: English normally puts a plural noun after any number larger than one. Russian makes a distinction between два стола́ and пять столо́в. It also remembers the gender of an omitted noun: две still refers to feminine кни́ги. With the noun left out, Russian says the number alone: У меня́ две.

examples.text: У тебя одна книга, а у меня две.
examples.means: You have one book, and I have two.
examples.literal: At you one book, and at me two.

contrasts.says: Пять книг uses the plural genitive. Две кни́ги uses the singular genitive even though two books are meant.
The choice of оди́н or одна́, and of два or две, follows the noun, not the person who owns it.

mistakes.why: After два, стол takes its genitive singular form стола́.
Пять needs the genitive plural, not the prepositional plural кни́гах.
Кни́га is feminine, so one is одна́.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

chtoby.explain: First say what someone does, then give the purpose with что́бы and an infinitive: Я иду́ в парк, что́бы безопа́сно гуля́ть. The person going is also the person walking, so no second subject is needed. The purpose can describe an activity, гуля́ть, or a bounded result, отдохну́ть. Что́бы does not automatically require one aspect. In Останови́сь здесь, что́бы позвони́ть ма́ме, both actions concern the person addressed. A comma separates the main action from its purpose. A different person in the purpose clause needs a construction taught in a later round.
chtoby.why: English often expresses purpose with to alone: go home to rest. Russian can say it with что́бы, which these lessons use; after a verb of going, a bare infinitive works too: Мы идём домо́й отдохну́ть. This differs from an infinitive directly after хочу́ or могу́, where no purpose connector is needed. It also differs from потому́ что, which explains a cause.

examples.text: Я иду в парк, чтобы безопасно гулять.
examples.means: I'm going to the park to walk safely.
examples.literal: I go to park, in order to safely walk.
Stop here, in order to call to Mom.
We go home, in order to rest.

contrasts.says: Потому́ что introduces the reason something happens. Что́бы introduces the intended purpose; that purpose need not already be achieved.
Я хочу́ отдохну́ть has an infinitive directly after хочу́. Мы идём домо́й, что́бы отдохну́ть adds the purpose of going home.

mistakes.why: For this same-person purpose, use an infinitive, not the present-tense form отдыха́ем.

mistakes.wrong: Я иду́ в парк, что́бы безопа́сно гуля́ю.
mistakes.right: Я иду́ в парк, что́бы безопа́сно гуля́ть.
mistakes.why: Гуля́ю is a finite present form. The purpose here needs the infinitive гуля́ть.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

pronoun-cases.explain: The six cases give a pronoun different jobs. Я is nominative, the subject. У меня́ uses genitive for the holder; ждёт меня́ uses accusative for the person awaited. Помога́ет мне uses dative for the recipient. Со мной uses instrumental for a companion; обо мне uses prepositional for a topic. The same spelling мне has two jobs: the surrounding words tell you which. For ты, compare ты, тебя́, тебе́, тобо́й. For мы, familiar нас becomes нам for a recipient and на́ми after с. For вы, use вас, вам or ва́ми as needed. Learn the form with the verb or preposition. The preposition обо is unstressed in обо мне; the stress falls on мне. Third-person forms after prepositions come later.
pronoun-cases.why: English keeps you in I see you, I help you and with you. Russian distinguishes тебя́, тебе́ and тобо́й. English me also covers both мне and меня́. These forms show the role even when the order changes; they are not interchangeable just because English uses the same word.

examples.text: Ты мне помогаешь, а я тебе.
examples.means: You help me, and I help you.
examples.literal: You to me help, and I to you.

examples.text: Это для тебя, а не для меня.
examples.means: This is for you, not for me.
examples.literal: This for you, and not for me.

examples.text: Мама ждёт меня, а не тебя.
examples.means: Mom is waiting for me, not you.
examples.literal: Mom waits for me, and not you.

examples.means: She wants to talk to me.

contrasts.says: Меня́ and тебя́ name a direct object in ждёт меня́ or ви́дит тебя́. The full set also includes мне and тебе́ for recipients and мной and тобо́й for companions.
Мне in помога́ет мне is dative. The identical мне in обо мне is prepositional: обо selects that case.
Use тебе́ and тобо́й with a friend. For polite or plural вы, familiar вам and ва́ми fill these roles: помо́чь вам, с ва́ми.

mistakes.why: Помога́ть takes the dative recipient мне, not the accusative меня́.
After обо for the topic, use prepositional мне.
After со for a companion, use instrumental мной, not subject я.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

reflexive.explain: The ending -ся or -сь is part of the verb, not a separate pronoun. Change the person before it: я бою́сь, ты бои́шься, он бои́тся. In these forms, -сь follows a vowel and -ся a consonant letter or the soft sign ь. The label reflexive does not mean every verb translates with yourself: боя́ться means be afraid, учи́ться means learn or study, and начина́ться means begin. Some verbs describe something done to oneself, some mutual contact, some a state or event. Learn each whole verb, its meaning and any case or preposition it needs; adding -ся freely does not guarantee a word with the intended meaning. Watch spelling in verbs like боя́ться: the infinitive has -ться, the third-person form -тся (он бои́тся). The phone-call lesson later practices mutual contact.
reflexive.why: English often uses a plain verb or be plus an adjective where Russian has a verb in -ся: Я бою́сь means I am afraid; Я учу́сь means I am learning. Do not add a separate yourself to every English translation. The whole Russian word carries the meaning.

examples.means: I’m afraid to watch this film.
examples.literal: I am afraid watch this film.

examples.means: My sister is afraid to watch too.

contrasts.says: The person still matters: я бою́сь, ты бои́шься. Keeping -ся or -сь does not replace the ordinary person endings.
Do not confuse the soft sign of an infinitive in -ться with a third-person form in -тся. Compare the dictionary verb боя́ться with он бои́тся.
The ending does not choose aspect: учи́ться describes learning, while познако́миться presents becoming acquainted as a whole event. Learn aspect with the verb too.

mistakes.why: For я, use бою́сь; бои́шься goes with ты. Keep the reflexive ending.
The third-person form бои́тся has no soft sign before -ся. This is a verb-form spelling error, not a different aspect.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

li.explain: After know, want to know or check, a question can become part of a larger sentence. If the question asks where, keep где: Ты зна́ешь, где мой телефо́н? If it asks for yes or no, use ли. Put the questioned word or group before ли: до́ма ли сестра́, рабо́тает ли А́нна, пра́вильно ли я записа́л и́мя. This lesson uses simple one-word focuses. Ли cannot introduce the clause from the front like English whether. Put a comma before the embedded question. The ending of the verb still agrees with its own subject. English if can also mean whether here; this is not a conditional sentence.
li.why: English puts whether or if before the whole embedded clause. Russian puts ли after the word or group it questions. Where is different: it asks for a location, so где stays. A statement with что says what is believed or known; a clause with ли leaves a yes/no question open.

examples.means: Do you know where my phone is?

examples.text: Я не знаю, дома ли сестра.
examples.means: I don’t know whether my sister is home.
examples.literal: I not know, at home whether sister.

examples.text: Ты знаешь, работает ли Анна сегодня?
examples.means: Do you know whether Anna is working today?
examples.literal: You know, works whether Anna today?

examples.text: Я не знаю, есть ли у тебя время.
examples.means: I don’t know whether you have time.
examples.literal: I not know, is whether at you time.

examples.text: Проверь, правильно ли я записал имя.
examples.means: Check whether I wrote the name down correctly.
examples.literal: Check, correctly whether I wrote down name.

contrasts.says: Где asks for a place, so it stays at the start of the embedded question. Ли marks a yes/no question and follows its focus.
Я зна́ю, что сестра́ до́ма states that she is home. Я не зна́ю, до́ма ли сестра́ leaves that question open.

mistakes.wrong: Я не зна́ю, ли до́ма сестра́.
mistakes.right: Я не зна́ю, до́ма ли сестра́.
mistakes.why: Ли follows the questioned до́ма; it does not begin the clause.

mistakes.wrong: Прове́рь, ли пра́вильно я записа́л и́мя.
mistakes.right: Прове́рь, пра́вильно ли я записа́л и́мя.
mistakes.why: Put ли after пра́вильно, the point being checked.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

conditional.explain: Бы with a past-form verb expresses a wish, an imagined possibility or a softened request. Вы могли́ бы мне помо́чь? asks for help now, not about past ability. The verb still agrees: a man says Я хоте́л бы помо́чь, a woman Я хоте́ла бы помо́чь; with мы or вы, use хоте́ли бы or могли́ бы. Write бы separately. It can follow the verb or come earlier: Я хоте́л бы спроси́ть and Я бы хоте́л спроси́ть are both natural. After хоте́л бы or мог бы, another action takes the infinitive. Keep ты with a friend and вы with an unfamiliar adult. Adding бы does not make ты a formal form of address.
conditional.why: English uses would like or could for these wishes and requests. Russian combines a past-form verb with бы, so its gender or plural ending remains visible even when the wish concerns now or tomorrow. Вы не могли́ бы повтори́ть? is a conventional polite request; the negative wording does not mean the speaker wants no repetition.

examples.literal: You could would to me help?
I wanted would help to you.

examples.text: Я хотела бы поговорить с вами.
examples.means: I'd like to talk to you.
examples.literal: I wanted would talk with you.

examples.text: Я бы хотел спросить о работе.
examples.means: I'd like to ask about work.
examples.literal: I would wanted ask about work.

contrasts.says: The past form supplies the agreement, but бы changes the meaning: Я хоте́л бы помо́чь is a present wish, not a statement that the speaker wanted to help earlier.
Only the first verb has the past-form ending: Я хоте́л бы помо́чь. The second action is an infinitive.
Вы могли́ бы помо́чь? addresses an unfamiliar adult politely. Ты мог бы помо́чь? addresses a male friend; to a female friend, Ты могла́ бы помо́чь?

mistakes.why: Бы does not remove agreement. With мы, use plural могли́, not singular мог.
After хоте́л бы, use an infinitive for the intended action. Помога́ю is a finite present form.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

impersonal.explain: Some sentences have no nominative subject. In Мне удо́бно учи́ться до́ма, мне names the person for whom studying at home works well. Use dative мне, тебе́, нам or вам, and keep удо́бно unchanged. Ну́жно with an infinitive expresses a need: Мне ну́жно учи́ться. Тру́дно describes difficulty in the same way. The person can be left understood: Мо́жно учи́ться вме́сте expresses permission or possibility. Do not insert a Russian word for it just because English says it is convenient or it is possible. Learn the describing word and the construction together.
impersonal.why: English often makes I or you the subject: I need to study, or I find studying difficult. Russian can instead name the person in the dative and describe the need or experience without a subject. This pattern does not make every noun after мне an object: in Мне нужна́ кни́га, кни́га is the subject and нужна́ agrees with it.

examples.means: Studying at home works well for me.
examples.literal: To me convenient study at home.

examples.means: Is it comfortable for you to read on your phone?
examples.literal: To you comfortable read on phone?

examples.means: Studying in the evening suits me.
examples.literal: To me convenient study in the evening.

examples.means: We can study together after work.

contrasts.says: Ну́жно with an infinitive stays unchanged: Мне ну́жно учи́ться. With a noun as subject, the short adjective agrees: Мне нужна́ кни́га; Мне ну́жен телефо́н.
Мне and тебе́ name the person experiencing the need or difficulty. They are not subject forms я and ты.
The activity after удо́бно or мо́жно is an infinitive: Мне удо́бно чита́ть; Мо́жно учи́ться вме́сте.

mistakes.why: For the person experiencing this convenience, use dative мне. Я is a subject form and does not fit this construction.
After ну́жно, use the infinitive учи́ться, not the finite present учу́сь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 101–120, open to correction.
